stories.headline: Fed minutes show more worry about prices, and three people already wanted a hike
stories.dek: July meeting notes, released Wednesday, say several officials were ready to raise rates.
stories.caveman: The Fed is the US money boss. They pick how expensive it is to borrow. In late July they left the rate where it was, between 3.50 and 3.75 percent. Three people on the team voted no. They wanted a tiny hike. On Wednesday the Fed published the secret notes from that meeting. The notes say more people are scared prices will stay high, especially because oil is messy after the Iran war. The notes also say many officials think a hike will be needed later if prices do not cool toward 2 percent. Markets barely jumped. People already guessed this.
stories.why_it_matters: These notes are old news from July, but they tell you the Fed is twitchy. If oil stays high, your loan and credit card can get more expensive this fall.
stories.camps: Hawks say wait too long and you need a bigger, meaner hike later. Doves say the July jobs report, which came after the meeting, was weak, so slamming the brakes now could hurt workers. Trump wants cheaper gas for the midterms.

terms.explain: The US central bank. They set the main interest rate.
The price of borrowing money. Higher rate means loans cost more.
The official notes of a meeting, published later so people can see how they argued.
Prices going up. Same money buys less cabbage.

stories.headline: US and Indian fuel sellers are making a pile while wars scramble diesel
stories.dek: Reuters: US distillate exports hit a record as diesel at the pump sits near $5.47 a gallon.
stories.caveman: Two wars, Iran and Ukraine, broke some of the usual fuel pipes. Refineries in the US and India are cooking more diesel and jet fuel and selling it abroad. In one recent week US distillate exports hit about 1.9 million barrels a day, a record. AAA says US diesel at the pump was about $5.47 a gallon on Tuesday, almost 50 percent higher than last year. Trump wants cheaper gas at home before November votes. The White House has even muttered about export limits, which traders say could slam prices fast.
stories.why_it_matters: If you drive a truck or heat with oil, this is your wallet. If Washington limits exports to make home prices look nicer, other countries get squeezed.
stories.camps: Refiners and their shareholders like the fat margins. Drivers and the White House want cheaper pumps. Importers in Asia and Europe pay up or go without.

terms.explain: A factory that turns crude oil into gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel.
A family of fuels that includes diesel and heating oil.
A US drivers club that tracks pump prices.

stories.headline: The US Treasury said it will buy back twice as much long-term debt
stories.dek: The announcement, the same Wednesday as the Fed minutes, eased bond yields and helped stocks after Tuesday's drop.
stories.caveman: The US government owes a mountain of money. Some of that mountain is long-term bonds, IOUs that last many years. When lots of people sell those bonds, the yield, the interest the government must pay, goes up. On Wednesday the Treasury said it will double how much of that long-term paper it buys back. Buying back means the government itself is a customer, which can calm the market. Yields eased a bit and stocks got a lift after a rough Tuesday.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a plumber move on a clogged pipe. It does not make the debt smaller in a simple way. It can stop a panic in bond land from spilling into your mortgage rate.
stories.camps: The Treasury says this is plumbing, not a rescue. Skeptics say the government is propping up its own paper because private buyers got picky.

terms.explain: The US money ministry. They collect taxes and sell bonds.
The government buys its own old IOUs so fewer sit in the market.
The interest a bond pays. When yields jump, new borrowing gets pricier.

stories.headline: Brent oil sat near $91 as Fed notes admitted Hormuz has messed up the inflation map
stories.dek: Minutes say the Iran war 'materially complicated' prices. Brent is higher than the July data the Fed was reading.
stories.caveman: Think of Hormuz as a skinny door for a fifth of the world's seaborne oil. That door has been half shut for months. Brent, the world's main oil price tag, sat near 91 dollars a barrel this week. The Fed's July notes, published Wednesday, say the fight has made their inflation job harder. The joke is the notes describe a world before this week's oil jump. So the Fed is driving with an old map.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil in the 90s can leak into food, shipping, and then into the Fed's next hike. Taiwan feels it too when shipping and fuel cost more.
stories.camps: Hawks say this is why you hike. Iran says the strait stays shut until the US lifts sanctions. Trump says the strait is open and the blockade stays.

terms.explain: The main world oil price, named after a North Sea field.
A skinny sea door by Iran. A lot of the world's oil boats go through it.

stories.headline: OpenAI will watch for bad users without keeping their words
stories.dek: TechCrunch, Aug 19: a preview called Private Safety Processing, meant to one-up Anthropic's 30-day keep-the-chats rule.
stories.caveman: OpenAI sells brain-in-a-box to companies. Those companies hate the idea that OpenAI staff can read their secrets. So OpenAI already offered Zero Data Retention: we look, we answer, we forget. The problem is bad guys can hide a crime across many little chats. OpenAI now previews a robot that looks across chats for a pattern, then only pings OpenAI with a tiny alarm, not the actual words. Anthropic, the rival, said it will keep chats for 30 days on its strongest models. Unpopular, they admit, but they say they need it.
stories.why_it_matters: If you run a company, this is the new privacy sales pitch. If you worry about AI helping hackers, you want someone to actually see the trail. Those two wants fight.
stories.camps: OpenAI says forget-the-words can still catch multi-step abuse. Anthropic says you cannot catch sophisticated attacks if you throw the tape away. Regular ChatGPT users are not in this program yet.

terms.explain: The company behind ChatGPT.
A rival AI company. Their chatbot is Claude.
A promise: after the answer, we do not keep your prompt.

stories.headline: OpenAI accidentally kicked security researchers out of its cyber club
stories.dek: TechCrunch, Aug 19: a bug revoked Daybreak Blue access. Many of the people who complained live outside the US and Europe.
stories.caveman: OpenAI has a special door for trusted hackers-for-good. It is called Trusted Access for Cyber, nickname Daybreak. Behind that door, the robot is allowed to help find bugs and study malware. On Wednesday a bunch of those researchers opened the door and got a slap: identity not verified, or you are ineligible. OpenAI said oops, technical issue, please sign up again. The people TechCrunch talked to were not in the US or Europe.
stories.why_it_matters: If the good-guy hackers cannot get in, the bad guys still try. A flaky door also makes people wonder whether the club is quietly shrinking.
stories.camps: OpenAI says it was a bug, not a punishment. Researchers outside the West wonder if the map of who is trusted just got smaller.

terms.explain: OpenAI's club for approved cybersecurity researchers.
Bad software that breaks or spies on computers.

stories.headline: Meta put its chatbot on the Mac so it can see your screen
stories.dek: The Verge, Aug 19: a desktop app that can look at a window, talk to Instagram and ads, and type by voice.
stories.caveman: Meta is the Facebook and Instagram company. They already have a chatbot in the phone. Now there is a Mac app. You can share a window so the bot sees what you see. It can also hook to Google Workspace and to your Facebook or Instagram business tools, then suggest what to post, or make a deck. OpenAI and Anthropic already let their bots drive the computer more aggressively. Meta is late, and a bit softer. It looks, it suggests, it does not fully grab the wheel the way those two can.
stories.why_it_matters: More bots on the desktop means more of your work day is watched by a company that already knows your friends list. Handy for a small shop. Creepy if you forget the window is shared.
stories.camps: Meta says this is a work helper. Privacy people will ask what leaves the machine. Apple will care that another company's eyes sit on the Mac.

terms.explain: The company that owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.
A program that lives on an Apple computer, not just in a browser.

stories.headline: Google stuffed Search and Gemini with study toys for students
stories.dek: TechCrunch, Aug 19: 3D simulations, quizzes, a student hub, and reports that cook in the background.
stories.caveman: Google wants the homework helper crown. On Wednesday it added study tools to Search and Gemini. You can get a 3D model of DNA you can spin. You can get a quiz. You can tell Gemini to write a research report, close the chat, and get a ping when it is done. There is a new hub that keeps notebooks and flashcards in one pile. OpenAI and little homework apps are in the same fight.
stories.why_it_matters: Kids will use this. Teachers will have to decide if spinning DNA is learning or a shortcut. Schools that already live in Google Classroom just got another hook.
stories.camps: Google says this helps you understand. Critics will say it writes the paper while you watch a 3D cartoon.

terms.explain: Google's chatbot.
Google's main box for looking things up.

stories.image_alt: Google study tools or Gemini image

stories.headline: Trump leans on a longer squeeze of Iran after the 60-day clock died
stories.dek: ABC and others, Aug 19: no hurry for a deal, new sanctions teased, maybe even on bigger Chinese banks.
stories.caveman: The short peace memo with Iran ran out Monday. Trump now says he is not in a hurry. His energy secretary calls it the long game. Treasury has talked about never-seen sanctions. One idea on the table: punish bigger Chinese banks that help buy Iranian oil. Some US officials like that. Some say Beijing will hit back and it is not worth it. Iran says the strait stays shut until the US lifts the blockade and unfreezes money. Analysts say Iran is more likely to poke Gulf allies than to tap out.
stories.why_it_matters: A long squeeze means oil stays jumpy and talks stay dead. Taiwan sits on the other end of those shipping lanes.
stories.camps: Trump's team says time and money will bend Tehran. Iran says this is not surrender dressed up as talks. China has not been fully targeted yet because the blowback scare is real.

terms.explain: Rules that block money or trade to hurt a country or company.
Punishing someone else's bank or buyer for dealing with the first target.

stories.headline: Ukraine and Russia each sent 103 prisoners home, with the UAE in the middle
stories.dek: Reuters, Aug 19: 206 people swapped. Kyiv says another swap may come this month, including Mariupol defenders.
stories.caveman: War is still on. But both sides sometimes trade people they captured. On Wednesday each side sent 103 prisoners home. The United Arab Emirates helped set the table. That country has now midwifed 26 of these trades, almost 8,000 people in all. Zelensky said the Ukrainians include army, border guards, and national guard, some from Mariupol. Some are hurt or sick. The oldest is 59. The youngest was born in 2000. Ukraine's intel chief says they want a longer-held group next.
stories.why_it_matters: A swap is not peace. It is a small human door in a locked war. Families get someone back. The front does not move.
stories.camps: Kyiv and Moscow stay far apart on a real deal. Both still like the UAE as a phone book. Putin thanked Abu Dhabi. Zelensky thanked the people who keep filling the exchange list.

terms.explain: Prisoner of war. A soldier captured by the other side.
United Arab Emirates. A Gulf country that has been brokering these swaps.
A Ukrainian port Russia surrounded early in the 2022 invasion.

stories.headline: A Russian drone hit a police building in Zhytomyr. Two died, about 20 were hurt
stories.dek: Kyiv Independent, Aug 19: one piece of a day that also killed 17 people across Ukraine.
stories.caveman: Zhytomyr is a city west of Kyiv, not the front line. A drone hit the police headquarters. Two people died. At least 20 were hurt. Across the country that day, Ukrainian officials counted 17 dead and 54 hurt from Russian attacks, including a minibus in Kherson. Ukraine said its own drones hit energy and factory sites inside Russia. So both sides are still throwing metal at cities far from the trench.
stories.why_it_matters: When a police HQ in the rear burns, it means the war is not only a map of the east. It is also a contest over who can scare the other side's ordinary towns.
stories.camps: Russia calls these strikes on military or energy targets. Ukraine calls them terror on civilians. Independent counts are hard in the dark.

terms.explain: A flying robot, often with a bomb.
A Ukrainian city west of Kyiv.

stories.headline: Iran called a Ukrainian hit on a ship in the Caspian a terrorist act
stories.dek: Iran International, Aug 19: Tehran's ambassador in Russia said the strike on an Iranian vessel was deliberate.
stories.caveman: The Caspian is a big inland sea north of Iran. Ukraine hit an Iranian ship there, Iran says. The ambassador in Moscow called it terrorism. This sits next to Trump saying no talks are scheduled and the US blockade stays. Iran's speaker says Hormuz stays closed until Washington does what the June memo promised. So the war is not only in the Gulf. It is leaking into other waters and other friendships, Iran and Russia sharing a sea.
stories.why_it_matters: A ship hit in the Caspian is a reminder the Iran fight has extra rooms. Each room can drag in another country.
stories.camps: Iran says Ukraine crossed a line. Ukraine has been hitting anything that helps Russia's war machine. The US is not a party to that ship story, but the timing sits inside the dead Iran talks.

terms.explain: A huge lake-like sea between Iran and Russia. Ships move oil and cargo there.

stories.headline: A tradwife-goes-to-1855 novel is the book US indie shops cannot keep
stories.dek: IndieBound list for Aug 19: Caro Claire Burke's Yesteryear is number one. Ann Patchett's Whistler is number two.
stories.caveman: Independent bookstores make their own bestseller list. This week the top novel is Yesteryear. A modern 'tradwife' influencer, the kind of internet woman who performs old-fashioned housewife life, wakes up in 1855 and has to figure out if it is a trick, a TV show, or real. It was the number one Indie Next pick back in April and it is still eating the table. Right under it is Ann Patchett's Whistler, a quieter book about how life does not last and friends do.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the 'who is hot' snapshot. Not TikTok romantasy this time. Indies are selling a satire of online femininity and a beloved literary name at once.
stories.camps: Some readers want the tradwife nightmare as a joke on the algorithm. Some just want Patchett to hold their hand. Both are winning in small shops.

terms.explain: A social-media style where a woman performs 1950s-housewife life as content.
The bestseller list from independent US bookstores, not Amazon.
A famous American novelist. People trust her the way they trust a good teacher.

stories.image_alt: Yesteryear or indie bestseller display

stories.headline: Penguin Random House froze a book about Zohran Mamdani after plagiarism claims
stories.dek: Washington Post via Editor and Publisher, Aug 19: Ross Barkan's The Revolutionary is off Amazon and the big stores.
stories.caveman: Zohran Mamdani is New York City's mayor. A journalist, Ross Barkan, wrote a book about him called The Revolutionary, due in October. This week the publisher, Penguin Random House, stopped selling and promoting it. People had said Barkan copied a lot in old New York Magazine columns. By Monday the book pages were gone from Amazon, Barnes and Noble, Target, and Walmart. He had been asking readers to preorder it.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the literary world's trust test. A hot political book can die before it ships if the author's old work looks stolen. Huiru has been watching Mamdani and NYC labor. The book about him just got locked in the basement.
stories.camps: The publisher is protecting its name. Barkan's side, if he has one in public, is not the lead of this report. Bookstores just pulled the listing.
stories.source_name: The Washington Post / Editor and Publisher

terms.explain: One of the biggest book publishers on earth.
Copying someone else's words and pretending they are yours.
New York City's mayor as of 2026. Came out of the city's left.

stories.headline: Colson Whitehead's 1980s Harlem novel is climbing the indie list
stories.dek: IndieBound Aug 19: Cool Machine, book three of the Harlem Trilogy, is an August Indie Next pick.
stories.caveman: Colson Whitehead has two Pulitzer prizes. He is writing a trio of books about Harlem. The new one, Cool Machine, is set in 1980s New York and it is showing up on indie lists this week. If you do not know Harlem, think of a famous Black neighborhood in Manhattan with a huge arts and history pile. Whitehead likes to make that pile move.
stories.why_it_matters: When a Pulitzer writer is mid-trilogy, book people treat it like a TV season drop. It is a 'who is hot' signal that is not BookTok.
stories.camps: Fans of literary fiction will follow the trilogy. Readers who only want romantasy will walk past. Both groups are in the same store this week.

terms.explain: An American novelist. Two Pulitzers. Often writes about Black American history with a grin.
A neighborhood in New York City, famous for Black art, music, and politics.

stories.image_alt: Cool Machine or Whitehead coverage

stories.headline: Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan's Trump book is the serious nonfiction on the table
stories.dek: IndieBound Aug 19: Regime Change sits high on regional lists. Two reporters who have followed Trump for a decade.
stories.caveman: Some people want novels. Some people want the longest Trump story they can stand. Regime Change, by New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman and journalist Jonathan Swan, is that pile this week. The subtitle frames it as a portrait of a radical presidency. It is not a beach romance. It is sitting next to David Sedaris essays in the same indie nonfiction row.
stories.why_it_matters: US book culture right now is split: escape novels on one table, Trump autopsy on the other. Both are selling.
stories.camps: Trump's fans will call it hostile. His critics will call it the record. The authors' claim is they were closer than most.

terms.explain: A New York Times reporter who has covered Trump for years.
A book that says it is about the real world, not made-up people.

stories.image_alt: Regime Change or political nonfiction display

stories.headline: The UN says 200,000 more people in Sudan were pushed from their homes, and floods are on top of the war
stories.dek: IOM, Aug 19: 8.6 million have fled since 2023. Hormuz and the Red Sea delays are now starving the aid pipeline too.
stories.caveman: Sudan's war is army versus a group called RSF. It has been going since April 2023. On Wednesday the UN migration agency said at least 200,000 more people have been newly displaced since late 2025, many in Kordofan. Floods wrecked about 1,350 shelters in one Darfur camp last week. In three days IOM still moved 1,750 tons of stuff, kits and tents, for more than 100,000 people. They say they need money for shelter or it gets worse. And because Hormuz and the Red Sea are a mess, the boats that bring aid are late.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the biggest displacement crises on earth. The Iran war is now a tax on Sudanese tents.
stories.camps: Aid groups want money and open roads. The two armed sides keep fighting. Donors are tired. None of that is a reason the numbers are small. They are not.

terms.explain: The UN's migration agency. They count displaced people and try to house them.
Forced to leave home, still maybe in the same country.
Rapid Support Forces. One of the two main armed sides in Sudan's war.

stories.image_alt: Sudan displacement or IOM aid image

stories.headline: About 11,000 people fled two North Kordofan villages in three days
stories.dek: IOM field teams, reported Aug 19: Umm Sumayma and Abu Haraz, Aug 16 to 18, after security got worse.
stories.caveman: Zoom in from the 200,000. In just three days, monitors think about 11,000 people ran from two villages in Sheikan, North Kordofan. The army said it shot down two drones in the state. This is what a 'surge' looks like when you stand in one county. Some earlier days in the same area already pushed out thousands more.
stories.why_it_matters: A three-day number that big means the war is not a slow leak. It is a burst. Those people need water today, not a conference in October.
stories.camps: The army talks about drones. Families talk about leaving. IOM is the one counting both.

terms.explain: A big region in the middle of Sudan. El Obeid is a main city there.

stories.image_alt: North Kordofan displacement image

stories.headline: Colombia's poor Pacific region is trying to stand up after a 7.4 quake
stories.dek: AP, Aug 19: at least 312 dead, 29,000 homes gone. Choco was already poor, under-built, and living with armed groups.
stories.caveman: A huge earthquake hit Colombia on Aug 10. The count by Wednesday: more than 300 dead, thousands hurt, tens of thousands of homes wrecked. The hardest luck is Choco, a mostly Afro-Colombian and Indigenous region that already had bad roads, weak hospitals, and fighters in the trees. A UN official called it a triple crisis: the quake, the old neglect, and the old conflict. About 10 percent of Choco's people were hit. Kids lost more than 200 schools. Traffickers, the UN migration agency warns, now sniff around the shelters.
stories.why_it_matters: Disaster aid that ignores the old poverty will rebuild the same trap. This is why the recovery is slower than a rich city would be.
stories.camps: Bogota promises an official and rent subsidies. Local doctors say they were empty-handed before the shaking started. Armed groups do not pause for rubble.

terms.explain: A poor, rainy region on Colombia's Pacific side.
A big earthquake number. Each step up is much stronger than the last.

stories.image_alt: Colombia earthquake aid sorting in Bogota

stories.headline: The UN is trying to feed 100,000 after that Colombia quake, and warns traffickers are already at the shelters
stories.dek: UN update around Aug 19: 186,000 affected, 304 dead in an earlier tally, 75,000 students without a safe school.
stories.caveman: Feeding people after a quake is a second job on top of pulling them from concrete. WFP, the World Food Programme, wants 23 million dollars to feed 100,000 people for three months. OCHA, another UN desk, says more than 186,000 people were affected and more than 26,500 homes destroyed. IOM says the chaos is catnip for traffickers who fake jobs and steal IDs. They told people: only trust official help.
stories.why_it_matters: Money and food are the boring part of saving lives. Without them the dramatic rescue week turns into a hungry month.
stories.camps: UN agencies want donors to write checks. Local officials want a rebuild that is not just tents. Criminal networks want a confused crowd.

terms.explain: World Food Programme. The UN's food truck.
Tricking or forcing people into work or sex. Disasters make it easier.
